conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in from your clinic visit because of nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve been so sick. The pain in my belly is constant—especially in the upper parts and around my G-tube. I’ve lost 32 pounds since I stopped TPN. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your G-tube isn’t draining much anymore—only about 300 cc a day. That’s less than before. We think it might not be working as well. We’re going to replace it today to help with the venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… will that hurt? I’m already in pain even with my morphine every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you some extra medication to keep you comfortable during the procedure. It’s done with imaging guidance, and we expect it to help reduce your nausea and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube was successfully replaced. We put in a shorter one with extra side holes, and it’s positioned well in your stomach. We hope this improves drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’m still nauseated. And I feel weak. I haven’t eaten in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your labs show low calcium and you’re malnourished. We’re working on getting you back on TPN, but we need insurance approval first. In the meantime, we’re giving IV fluids and supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m still nauseous. The promethazine helps a little, but not enough. Can we try something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adding ondansetron and ativan for nausea. We’re also continuing octreotide, which helps slow gut motility. We’ll monitor how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff, so we don’t think it’s an infection causing the nausea. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But my G-tube output is still low. Is that normal after the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s lower than we’d like. We’re concerned there might be a partial blockage at the stomach outlet. We’re discussing with GI whether we need to switch the tube type again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to change your G-tube again—this time to a Wills-Ogelsby tube. It’s designed to work better if there’s a blockage. We’ll do it early this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? How soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it for tomorrow. We want to make sure your stomach can drain properly so you feel less full and nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new Wills-Ogelsby tube is in. Output has already improved—now over 500 cc/day. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Less bloated. But I’m still tired and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’ve been malnourished. We’ve gotten approval for TPN. We’ll place a central line so you can receive it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of line? I’ve had port-a-caths before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This will be a tunneled femoral line in your left groin. It’s safer for now, given your history of clots and abdominal surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also checking your blood cultures to make sure there’s no infection. We’ll repeat them tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—both blood cultures are negative. No sign of infection in your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When will I start TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow. Once the line is placed, we’ll start slowly. You’ll continue it at home through this catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The femoral line was placed successfully. The tip is in the right spot in your vein. You can start TPN this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes time. You’ll start to gain strength and weight over the next few weeks. We’ll monitor your labs weekly to adjust the formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on dronabinol for nausea, but it makes me so sleepy. Can we stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discontinue it. The ondansetron and ativan seem to be helping, and we don’t want you overly drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My pain is still at my usual level—about 5 out of 10. I’m taking my gabapentin and morphine as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected with your condition. We’ll keep your pain regimen the same. We don’t want to increase sedation, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your calcium is improving with supplements. Your kidney function is stable, and your hemoglobin is slowly rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been using the walker like last time. I still feel unsteady sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue to encourage mobility. Physical therapy can reassess if needed, but you’re doing well walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re stable, on TPN, and your nausea is better controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home with TPN? How will I manage the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A visiting nurse will help at first. You’ll flush the line every eight hours and do an ethanol lock daily to prevent clots and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the TPN runs at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. From 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. We’ll send supplies and instructions. You’ll also take your usual meds, including octreotide and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your GI doctor and Dr. ___ regularly. And you need a chem-10 blood test every week—same day each week—and fax the results to Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time. I’ll make sure it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll also keep you on calcium, vitamin D, and your other supplements. Your hypothyroidism and Sjogren’s are stable—we’ll continue those meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling down. Not suicidal, but just… sad. Is that part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable. Chronic illness takes a toll. We’re continuing your Abilify, lamotrigine, and lorazepam. Please keep talking to your psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we changed your stomach acid medication back to Aciphex. We used ranitidine in the hospital, but you do better on your home regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I prefer it. Less heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You look well—alert, walking, and your abdomen is less tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more stable. Still weak, but better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. We’re discharging you home with visiting nurse support. They’ll help with TPN and line care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep taking all my meds as listed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Especially the TPN, octreotide, morphine for pain, and your psychiatric meds. Don’t stop anything without calling your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I get nauseous again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the promethazine suppository as needed. If it’s not helping, or if you have fever, redness at the line site, or can’t run TPN, call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help stabilize you. Take care, and keep up with your labs and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just want to feel stronger again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You will. It’ll take time, but you’re on the right path. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I watch for blood clots? I’ve had DVTs before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Watch for leg swelling or pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath. The ethanol lock helps reduce clot risk in the line. Stay as active as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay alert. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll make sure your home team has all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. The nurse will go over all instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse showed me how to do the ethanol lock. I think I’ve got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Consistency is key to keeping the line working and infection-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been very engaged in your care. That makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to stay healthy. This has been hard, but I’m hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. Keep up the good work. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re going home stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready too. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.
